sites.name: 1905 Mine
sites.location: Hurricane Hill / Boulder County Tungsten Mining District
overview: The 1905 Mine was a small but documented tungsten producer beside Hurricane Hill Road in the Boulder County tungsten district.
USGS records place the mine 825 feet south 25 degrees west of the Vasco No. 1 shaft and describe shaft workings associated with a ferberite-bearing vein along the Hurricane Hill breccia reef.

timeline.text: USGS indicates the mine may have produced tungsten before the surviving detailed production records begin.
The mine was productive during the World War I tungsten boom. Incomplete USGS records document about 250 units of WO3 from ore averaging 12.9 percent WO3.
USGS reported no known later production and estimated that total historic output may have exceeded 1,000 units of WO3.

moreHistory: U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 245 describes the 1905 Mine at roughly 8,550 feet elevation beside Hurricane Hill Road. The documented position is relative to the Vasco No. 1 shaft, which provides a defensible historic mine-level Scan anchor while avoiding a claim that the exact shaft collar has been surveyed by Remnant.

The mine was developed by shaft workings that USGS believed were probably no more than about 150 feet deep. The vein lies in the hanging wall of the Hurricane Hill breccia reef, striking roughly northeast and dipping northwest through aplite and granite.

USGS attributes the property to Gold, Silver, & Tungsten, Inc. during the documented production period. The retained production figures are incomplete, so Remnant presents them as reported historical estimates rather than precise lifetime totals.

sites.name: Acme Mine
overview: The Acme Mine was a major Louisville-area coal mine that operated from the late nineteenth century into 1928 and helped shape the town's industrial landscape.
Historic state and local records document deep shaft workings, company housing, railroad service, and repeated subsidence effects beneath Louisville.

timeline.text: The Acme Mine entered operation in Louisville during the expansion of Boulder County's northern coal field.
Colorado's coal-mine inspector described the Acme as a two-shaft mine about 190 feet deep, connected to the Colorado & Southern Railroad.
Rocky Mountain Fuel Company acquired the Acme and operated it through its final years.
Industrial Commission records document 81 Acme employees in a wage case involving Rocky Mountain Fuel Company.
The Acme Mine closed after decades of coal production beneath and around Louisville.

moreHistory: Colorado mine-inspector records describe a main shaft and air shaft serving a roughly six-foot coal seam, with the main shaft divided for hoisting, pipe lines, and emergency access.
Local historical records preserve 1911 photographs of the Rocky Mountain Fuel Company's Acme Mine and company houses, confirming the mine's substantial surface plant and community setting.
Historic Louisville research also documents subsidence associated with Acme workings beneath the town, showing how the mine's underground footprint affected the later urban landscape.

For Remnant identification, the USGS/GNIS mine point at approximately 39.98193, -105.13665 is used as the documented mine-level anchor rather than claiming a surviving shaft collar has been field-surveyed.

sites.name: Caribou Ghost Town
overview: Caribou is a high-elevation ghost town northwest of Nederland that grew beside one of Boulder County's best-known nineteenth-century silver districts.

The settlement developed rapidly after rich silver discoveries on Caribou Hill in 1869, and surviving historical records document a substantial mining community shaped by repeated fires, epidemics, and the collapse of silver mining in the 1890s.

timeline.text: Prospectors identified rich silver-bearing veins on Caribou Hill, including the Caribou and Poorman lodes, triggering rapid development of the district.
A town had formed at Caribou; a federal mining history reported about 30 houses and 125 voters by November.
A major fire swept through Caribou, one of several disasters that damaged the settlement during its mining years.
The silver-price collapse and financial panic forced most mines in the district to close, accelerating Caribou's decline.
Another major fire struck the town, further reducing the surviving building stock.

moreHistory: U.S. Geological Survey histories describe the Grand Island-Caribou area as a silver district west of Boulder and northwest of Nederland. By the end of 1871, most of the richest lodes had been located and production had expanded rapidly.

Late-1870s photographs preserved by the Carnegie Library for Local History show Caribou as a developed mountain settlement. The archive identifies the Sherman House in one view and notes additional views by William Henry Jackson.
Caribou Ghost Town is distinct from the nearby Caribou Mine, Caribou Ranch, and later recording-studio history. The townsite is represented separately as the historic settlement itself.

sites.name: Denver, Boulder & Western Railway / Switzerland Trail of America
overview: The Switzerland Trail follows portions of a historic narrow-gauge railroad corridor that served Boulder County mining communities and later became a well-known scenic excursion route.

timeline.text: Early narrow-gauge construction linked Boulder County mining districts, and the route expanded through the mountain communities west of Boulder.
The Colorado and Northwestern promoted the mountain railroad as the Switzerland Trail of America to attract excursion traffic as well as mining-related business.
Rail service ended and the tracks were removed, leaving substantial portions of the former railroad grade in the landscape.
The Denver, Boulder and Western Railway Historic District, also known as the Switzerland Trail of America, was listed in the National Register of Historic Places.

moreHistory: The corridor was used by several narrow-gauge railroad companies, including the Greeley, Salt Lake and Pacific Railway, Colorado and Northwestern Railroad, and Denver, Boulder and Western Railroad. It carried ore, supplies, residents, and tourists through Boulder County's mountain mining country.

Boulder County continues to recognize the Switzerland Trail railroad line as an important part of the county's mining and transportation history. Portions of the historic roadbed remain visible and are used for modern recreation.

sites.name: Conger Mine
sites.location: Sherwood Creek / west of Mud Lake near Nederland
overview: The Conger Mine was the leading tungsten mine of the Boulder County tungsten district near Nederland, developed after Samuel Conger and J. H. Wanamaker recognized valuable ferberite ore around 1900.

Federal mining records describe a 991-foot shaft and an extensive underground system, while modern Boulder County restoration work still identifies the historic mine site along Sherwood Creek west of Mud Lake.

timeline.text: Conger and Wanamaker recovered about 40 tons of high-grade tungsten ore from leased ground near Nederland, and Conger identified the vein that became the district's most productive.
After the original lease ended, the property was expanded into a major tungsten operation as demand for tungsten steel increased.
The mine grew into one of the most important producers in the district during the tungsten boom associated with high-speed steel and World War I demand.
USGS estimates indicate that the Conger Mine supplied roughly 20 to 25 percent of the Boulder County district's historic tungsten output.
Boulder County and Colorado reclamation agencies advanced work along Sherwood Creek to address mine waste and restore the stream corridor at the historic Conger site.

moreHistory: U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 245 describes the Conger as the most productive vein in the Boulder County tungsten district and documents the scale of the underground workings. The mine became a centerpiece of the Nederland-area tungsten industry that expanded rapidly after 1900.

The same federal history places the discovery in the period when tungsten steel was becoming important for high-speed cutting tools. Prices and demand rose sharply through the early twentieth century, culminating in the World War I boom.

The mine's legacy remains visible in the landscape. Boulder County identifies the Conger Mine site along Sherwood Creek, west of Mud Lake, where recent reclamation work has focused on mine waste and restoration of the creek corridor.

overview: Blue Jay Mine is a historic fluorspar mine southeast of Jamestown in Boulder County, where federal mining studies documented a substantial underground operation and Boulder County later preserved the site as a designated historic property.

timeline.text: Federal investigators described the Blue Jay Mine as developed by several short adits, a roughly 300-foot vertical shaft, and drifts on the 150- and 300-foot levels.
Federal teams sampled and examined the mine's lower workings during investigations of uranium-bearing minerals associated with the fluorite vein.
Boulder County designated Blue Jay Mine as a historic site, recognizing the surviving mining complex near Jamestown.

moreHistory: The Blue Jay vein was described by U.S. Geological Survey investigators as a northwest-trending structure more than 1,000 feet long, containing deep-purple crystalline fluorite with quartz, clay minerals, pyrite, galena, and uranium-bearing minerals.

Boulder County has described Blue Jay as one of the better-preserved and historically interesting mining complexes on its open-space properties. The surviving hoist-house area has also become important bat habitat, giving the historic mine an additional modern conservation role.

sites.name: Barker No. 3
sites.location: Boulder County Tungsten Mining District / Clark Tunnel area
overview: Barker No. 3 was a documented tungsten mine in Boulder County's historic tungsten district, developed through two surface shafts, adits, and a lower connection reached from the Clark Tunnel.

Colorado and U.S. Geological Survey records identify the property in the northeast quarter of Section 18, T1S R72W, and report production of at least about 6,000 units of tungsten concentrate during the district's active mining era.

timeline.text: Barker No. 3 was developed as part of the dense network of tungsten workings west of the former Tungsten settlement in Boulder County.
State and federal mine reports documented two upper shafts, an adit entering southwest of the shaft area, another caved adit, and a separate Clark Tunnel section with a drift and winze.

The same state report describes two distinct working sections. The upper section included two shafts, an adit entering from southwest of the shaft, and another adit that was already caved when documented. The lower Clark Tunnel section consisted of about 110 feet of drift on the vein and a 25-foot winze.

USGS Professional Paper 245 includes a plan of the Barker No. 3 workings and geologic surface sketch. Remnant uses an approximate historic mine-level identification point derived from the documented Barker No. 3/Vasco No. 6 spatial relationship; it does not claim that an individual shaft collar or surviving opening has been field-surveyed or is safe or accessible today.

sites.name: Boulder Valley Mine
overview: The Boulder Valley Mine was one of the defining coal mines of early Erie and, for a time, became Colorado's largest coal producer as railroad access expanded the Northern Coalfield.
The historic mine site lies near today's Coal Creek Disc Golf Course and the old Boulder Valley rail corridor, where the former workings helped shape Erie's growth as a coal town.

timeline.text: The Boulder Valley Railroad reached Erie, stimulating renewed development of the Northern Coalfield and a surge in production from the Boulder Valley Mine.
A miners' strike at the Boulder Valley Mine escalated during the episode remembered locally as the Erie War, and troops were brought in to maintain order.
Miners again struck for improved working conditions. The operating company removed machinery and abandoned the works after the strike continued.
The Boulder Valley Mine reopened under new ownership and remained part of Erie's coal-mining landscape.

moreHistory: Town of Erie historical material identifies the Boulder Valley Mine as a major early producer in the Northern Coalfield and links the mine directly to Erie's development as an important Colorado coal town.

Contemporary reporting and local interpretation note that the former entrance has been filled and mine structures no longer survive, while portions of the historic mining landscape remain visible near the route.

sites.name: Cardinal Mill & Mining Camp Complex
sites.location: Cardinal / Coon Track Creek west of Nederland
overview: Cardinal Mill is a rare surviving ore-concentration mill in western Boulder County, built beside the Boulder County Mine and the mining camp of Cardinal west of Nederland.

The mill processed gold and silver ore and later became an important tungsten mill, preserving an unusually complete example of the machinery and gravity-flow layout used in Colorado hard-rock mining.

timeline.text: Prospector Stephen Conger discovered the Boulder County lode, helping establish the mining activity that later supported the Cardinal settlement and mill complex.
The Cardinal Mill was built at the mouth of the Boulder County Tunnel as a gravity-flow concentration plant for local ore.
Cardinal operated as one of the region's full-time tungsten mills during Boulder County's early tungsten boom.
The mill returned to gold processing and operated intermittently until mining and milling ended in 1942.
Cardinal Mill was locally landmarked, acquired by Boulder County for preservation, and listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 2011.

moreHistory: Cardinal Mill was designed as a concentration plant on a steep slope above Coon Track Creek. Its stepped structure used gravity to move ore downward through successive treatment stages while reducing the amount of mechanical lifting required.

Boulder County records describe the mill as initially handling complex gold and silver ore from the Boulder County vein before operators shifted to tungsten. The plant later returned to gold processing and remained in intermittent use until 1942.

History Colorado identifies the Cardinal Mill as significant for engineering and industry and as an outstanding surviving concentration facility. Boulder County preservation work has retained the building and much of its historic milling equipment, making it an unusually intact example of the county's hard-rock mining infrastructure.

The surrounding Cardinal settlement developed around the mine, mill, and railroad connection, linking the industrial site to the broader mining community that occupied this part of western Boulder County.

sites.name: Invincible Mine
overview: Invincible Mine is a documented historic mine northwest of Jamestown that shifted from metal mining to fluorspar production during the early twentieth century.

timeline.text: A surviving Boulder Historical Society photograph documents the Invincible Mine near Jamestown and its mine building.

Fluorspar from the Invincible was among the Jamestown-district feed processed at the Valmont mill near Boulder for industrial use.

moreHistory: Colorado Geological Survey Bulletin 18 records that the Invincible had formerly been worked as a metalliferous mine before becoming an intermittent fluorspar producer. The report describes a persistent fluorite-rich vein and separate shaft, open-cut, tunnel and drift development.
Later federal work on the Jamestown fluorspar district retained the Invincible as a named mine and documented it within the district's broader fluorite system.

sites.name: Idaho Mine

moreHistory: USGS Professional Paper 94 identifies Idaho as one of the Caribou-area mines operating during the district's rapid 1870s development and preserves assay information for its early silver shipments.

sites.name: Chance Mine
sites.location: Beaver Creek area southeast of Nederland / Boulder County Tungsten Mining District
overview: Chance Mine, historically called the Tungsten Mine, was an important early tungsten property southeast of Nederland in Boulder County's tungsten district.

U.S. Geological Survey records trace the mine from the first discovery of the vein in 1900 through intensive early production, renewed underground development during World War I, and later federal-supported work.

timeline.text: Prospector Henry Loughlin discovered the Tungsten vein but made no recorded shipments.
John McRay sank a 15-foot shaft and mined a small quantity of ore.
Orin Beach developed and patented claims on the Tungsten vein; subsequent company operations reportedly recovered about $175,000 in ore before the early workings were thought exhausted.
George Cowdery explored eastward on the 120-foot level and found a new ore shoot, leading to further underground development.
Federal exploration records and Colorado mine reports continued to list the Tungsten (Chance) Mine as a tungsten property operated by Tungsten Mining Company.

moreHistory: U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 245 places the mine about 1 1/4 miles southeast of Nederland and about 3,300 feet west-southwest of Tungsten Mountain at roughly 8,530 feet elevation. The report describes the Tungsten and Chance names as referring to the same mine and documents its underground workings in detail.

The same federal history records early ore west of the shaft at very high reported tungsten grade and shows later development on deeper levels. A dedicated longitudinal projection of the Tungsten (Chance) workings was published from 1930 mine data.

A USGS/GNIS-derived mapped point for Tungsten Shaft at approximately 39.943598, -105.497775 is retained as a documented shaft-level component of the historic Tungsten/Chance mine. It is a historic mapped feature and does not imply that an open shaft or safe public access exists today.

overview: Evening Post Mine was a documented tungsten property at Switzerland Park in Boulder County's historic tungsten district, with separate tunnel and shaft workings developed on a short northeast-striking vein.

sites.name: Chancellor Mine
overview: Chancellor Mine is a documented producer in the Jamestown Mining District west of Jamestown, where fluorite mining became an important part of Boulder County's twentieth-century mineral industry.

U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 223 documented the Chancellor Mine among the Front Range ore deposits and retained it as a named Jamestown-district locality.

moreHistory: The Chancellor is also recorded as Allied Jamestown in mineral-locality references. Published records identify fluorite as a major commodity and also report silver, lead, and gold at the deposit.
The U.S. Bureau of Mines' 1949 Jamestown fluorite investigation describes drilling on the Chancellor vein as part of a broader study of mine workings and fluorspar resources in the district.

sites.name: Irene Mine

overview: The Irene Mine was a documented tungsten producer in Boulder County's tungsten district, about nine miles north of Nederland.

Colorado Geological Survey records describe a 150-foot shaft with two levels and an adit connecting to the 70-foot level, while USGS MRDS preserves a mine-level location for the Irene tungsten producer.

timeline.text: The Irene property was developed with a 150-foot shaft, two levels, and an adit that joined the 70-foot level.
Colorado Geological Survey records report production of five tons of ore averaging 0.89 percent tungsten oxide.
The property was recorded under owner and last operator J. E. Spaulding, with horn ore reported locally as running up to about 3 percent tungsten oxide.

sites.name: Boulder County Tunnel
sites.location: Coon Track Gulch below Cardinal / Grand Island Mining District
overview: The Boulder County Tunnel was a major nineteenth-century haulage and drainage tunnel driven from Coon Track Gulch below Cardinal to reach the Boulder County Mine and other Caribou-district workings.

Historic records show the project evolving from an ambitious district-scale tunnel in the 1870s into an operating mine-and-mill system, and surviving archival photography documents miners and equipment inside the tunnel near Cardinal.

timeline.text: The Consolidated Caribou Belt Mining Company began driving a roughly 7-by-7-foot tunnel from the bottom of Coon Track Gulch below Cardinal as a proposed drain and haulageway beneath the Caribou district.
The Boulder County Mining, Tunneling, Milling, Land & Town Company acquired the early tunnel and nearby water-powered mill and resumed development.

After the tunnel had reached about 700 feet, the operation changed ownership; later development completed the connection to the Boulder County Mine system and supported ore treatment at the adjacent mill.
Contemporary mining-industry reporting described the Boulder County Tunnel as having been advanced thousands of feet and working ore while the nearby Boulder County mill was being expanded.

moreHistory: History Colorado's National Register mining-context documentation describes the Boulder County Tunnel as an unusually ambitious early attempt to undercut the Caribou district, with compressed-air rock drills used to speed development.

The Carnegie Library for Local History preserves an undated Boulder Historical Society photograph taken inside the Boulder County Mine Tunnel near Cardinal, showing miners and equipment and identifying the site with the Grand Island Mining District.

USGS MRDS record 10141964 retains Boulder County Tunnel as a named underground mineral occurrence and identifies its mapped reference point as the main entrance. The coordinate is used by Remnant as a historic tunnel-level identification anchor, not as a claim that a surviving portal has been field-surveyed.

sites.name: Fair Day Mine
overview: The Fair Day Mine was Boulder County's most productive uranium mine and is a well-documented part of the Jamestown Mining District west of Jamestown.

Federal and Colorado geological reports trace uranium discovery at the Fair Day claim to 1955, underground development beginning in the late 1950s, and later work at both upper and lower mine levels on Overland Mountain.

timeline.text: Autunite and torbernite were identified in northeast-trending fractures on the Fair Day claim, establishing the uranium discovery at the mine site.
Diamond-core drilling during the fall and winter intersected a significant shallow uranium ore body.
An inclined shaft was sunk and production of uranium ore began.
USGS described an inclined shaft about 120 feet long, roughly 1,100 feet of drifts and crosscuts, and four stopes.
A lower adit was subsequently driven several hundred feet below the upper workings, creating another major mine level documented by later Colorado Geological Survey work.

moreHistory: USGS Bulletin 1159 identifies the Fair Day as the most productive uranium mine in Boulder County and places the historic upper workings about two miles west of Jamestown on the south side of Overland Mountain.

The Colorado Geological Survey later documented the lower Fair Day portal in detail while studying the site's geology, mining history, and environmental setting. Its report places the lower portal in Section 26, Township 2 North, Range 72 West, with the upper inclined-shaft workings higher on the mountain.

The retained mine-level coordinate marks the documented Fair Day Mine locality on Overland Mountain. The historic operation included multiple workings at different elevations, so visitors should treat the point as a mine-locality reference rather than a surveyed entrance to any particular opening.

sites.name: Emmett Mine

overview: The Emmett Mine was one of the major fluorspar producers in Boulder County's Jamestown Mining District, about a mile northwest of Jamestown on the south side of Little James Creek.

moreHistory: USGS describes the Emmett workings as a roughly 1,000-foot vertical shaft connected to a crosscut tunnel and ten levels, with the shaft collar lying in a large open cut. Several upper levels were already inaccessible when federal geologists examined the mine.

A federal 1944 Jamestown report includes dedicated geologic maps and sections of the Emmett Mine and Afterthought Tunnel, providing component-level evidence for the mine's identity and workings. The retained mine-level coordinate is treated as an identification point rather than a claim that a surviving shaft collar has been field-surveyed by Remnant.

sites.name: Balmoral
sites.location: About 900 feet east of Boulder Falls, Boulder County Tungsten Mining District
overview: The Balmoral Mine was a historic tungsten mine in Boulder County, about 900 feet east of Boulder Falls.
State and federal mining records document production, two connected shafts, multiple underground levels, and development on the Balmoral and Smith veins.

timeline.text: A detailed mine map of the Balmoral property was prepared for the Colorado Tungsten Corporation, documenting the property during the World War I-era tungsten-mining period.
USGS Professional Paper 245 records the mine as owned by Mrs. Washburn of Sugar Loaf and being worked by Hurlburt and Vant.
Colorado's Tungsten Mines of Colorado inventory reported about 1,500 units of production and summarized the mine's shafts, levels, veins, and remaining exploration potential.

moreHistory: The 1960 Colorado mine inventory places Balmoral in the southwest quarter of Section 36, Township 1 North, Range 72 West, about 900 feet east of Boulder Falls. It describes an inclined main shaft with levels at 16, 39, and 79 feet and a second shaft about 70 feet northeast that connected with the 39-foot level; both shafts were reported caved by that time.

USGS Professional Paper 245 reports that a stope at the shaft on the first level was said to have produced about $16,000 worth of ore, while another stope to the southwest yielded lower-grade material. Published records identify mineralization on the Balmoral and Smith veins.

The mapped identification point near 40.00667, -105.39806 is used as a site-level reference consistent with published Boulder County tungsten-district locality records and the documented position east of Boulder Falls. It should not be interpreted as a field-surveyed surviving shaft collar, property boundary, or statement of current access.

sites.name: Boulder County Tungsten District & Tungsten Ghost Town
overview: The Boulder County tungsten district became one of the most important tungsten-producing areas in the United States after ferberite mining began around 1900 west of Boulder.
The boom supported the settlement of Tungsten near present-day Barker Reservoir and tied the Nederland area to a nationally important strategic-metal industry during the early twentieth century.

timeline.text: USGS histories place the beginning of major tungsten mining in the Boulder County district around 1900.
Ferberite production expanded rapidly, and the district became a leading U.S. tungsten source during the World War I era.
Tungsten mining declined sharply after wartime demand fell, contributing to the decline of mining communities in the upper Boulder Creek watershed.

moreHistory: U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 245 documents the geology, claims, mines, and ore deposits of the Boulder County tungsten district and preserves detailed mapping of the district around Nederland and Barker Reservoir.

Boulder County historical interpretation identifies the former town of Tungsten near the area now occupied by Barker Reservoir and describes tungsten as one of the county's major historic mining industries.
This Remnant location represents the broader historic mining district and ghost-town landscape rather than a single tunnel portal or mine opening.
